mcqs.q: A mental disorder is a clinically significant disturbance in:
opts: Cognition, thinking, emotion, mood or behaviour
mcqs.explain: Mental disorders are disturbances in cognition, thinking, emotion regulation, mood or behaviour, causing distress, impaired function or risk of self-harm.

mcqs.q: The two most common mental disorders are:
mcqs.explain: Anxiety and depression are the most common mental disorders; depression affects about 264 million people worldwide.

mcqs.q: Why do patients with mental disorders have more caries and periodontal disease?
opts: Poor self-perception/neglected hygiene plus drug side effects and poor diet
mcqs.explain: Lack of perception of oral health, neglected hygiene, self-induced lesions, drug side effects, poor diet and substance abuse all raise the risk.

mcqs.q: Schizophrenia is characterised by:
opts: Impaired thought/perception/behaviour with loss of contact with reality (intelligence unimpaired)
mcqs.explain: Schizophrenia impairs thoughts, perceptions and behaviour with loss of contact with reality; intelligence is unimpaired and patients may know their behaviour is bizarre.

mcqs.q: Diagnosis of schizophrenia requires at least 2 persistent symptoms for:
mcqs.explain: Schizophrenia is diagnosed by ≥2 symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behaviour) persisting for 6 months.

mcqs.q: A delusion is best defined as:
opts: A false belief not subject to reason or evidence
Seeing things that are not there
mcqs.explain: A delusion is a false belief not amenable to reason/evidence; hallucinations are false perceptions (visual/auditory).

mcqs.q: 'Loose associations' and 'perseveration' are signs of:
mcqs.explain: Disorganized speech includes loose associations (rapidly shifting topics) and perseveration (repeating the same things).

mcqs.q: The most common dental complication in schizophrenia is:
mcqs.explain: Schizophrenic patients are at greater risk of caries, gingivitis and advanced periodontal disease, tooth loss and poor oral hygiene.

mcqs.q: Which class of drugs causes oral (tardive) dyskinesia?
mcqs.explain: Antipsychotics (especially phenothiazines like chlorpromazine) cause tardive dyskinesia after prolonged/high-dose use.

mcqs.q: Tardive dyskinesia affects about what proportion of patients on phenothiazines?
mcqs.explain: Tardive dyskinesia affects about 15–20% of patients on long-term phenothiazines, causing involuntary movements of the mouth, tongue, lips and jaws.

mcqs.q: An important feature of tardive dyskinesia is that it:
opts: Does NOT respond to withdrawal of the causative drug
Resolves instantly when the drug is stopped
mcqs.explain: Tardive dyskinesia does not respond to stopping the drug; management is to reduce the dose or switch to another antipsychotic such as clozapine.

mcqs.q: Haloperidol interacts with dental local anaesthesia by:
opts: Blocking the vasoconstrictor activity of adrenaline (epinephrine)
mcqs.explain: Haloperidol blocks the vasoconstrictor activity of adrenaline; it (and phenothiazines) also cause orthostatic hypotension, so raise the patient slowly.

mcqs.q: Combining an antipsychotic with tramadol carries a risk of:
mcqs.explain: With tramadol there is a risk of seizures in patients on antipsychotics; haloperidol/clozapine can also cause hypersalivation.

mcqs.q: Why should general anaesthesia be avoided if possible in a schizophrenic patient on antipsychotics?
mcqs.explain: GA can cause severe hypotension in patients on antipsychotics; conscious sedation, by contrast, is safe. Neuroleptics also intensify sedatives/opioids → respiratory depression.

mcqs.q: Patients on antipsychotics should be raised slowly from the dental chair because of:
mcqs.explain: Haloperidol and phenothiazines cause orthostatic hypotension, so the patient should be brought upright slowly.

mcqs.q: Depression is the ___ leading cause of disability and a risk factor for ___:
mcqs.explain: Depression is the 4th leading cause of disability and a risk factor for substance abuse, sleep disturbance, obesity and suicide.

mcqs.q: Major depression is diagnosed when persistent sadness/loss of interest lasts at least:
mcqs.explain: Major depression: persistent sad/empty mood and loss of interest for ≥2 weeks, with ≥4 of appetite/weight change, fatigue, guilt, poor concentration, disturbed sleep, suicidal thoughts.

mcqs.q: Depression is more common in females mainly due to:
mcqs.explain: Hormonal factors — menstrual changes, pregnancy, miscarriage and menopause — make depression commoner in women; it can also be genetic.

mcqs.q: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are relevant to dentistry because they:
opts: Potentiate the vasoconstrictor effect of epinephrine and cause xerostomia
Are completely safe in cardiac disease
mcqs.explain: TCAs potentiate epinephrine and cause xerostomia/constipation; they are contraindicated in cardiac disease, epilepsy, glaucoma and urinary obstruction.

mcqs.q: Which antidepressant class is associated with bruxism?
mcqs.explain: SSRIs cause xerostomia, stomatitis, glossitis and bruxism (and sexual dysfunction).

mcqs.q: Lithium (a mood stabiliser) causes which oral effects?
opts: Xerostomia, lichenoid stomatitis and a metallic taste
mcqs.explain: Lithium causes xerostomia (predisposing to candidiasis/caries), lichenoid stomatitis and a metallic taste.

mcqs.q: With MAOIs, which dental drug remains SAFE despite the tyramine 'cheese reaction'?
mcqs.explain: MAOIs interact dangerously with tyramine foods and ephedrine (hypertensive crisis), but epinephrine in LA can be used safely.

mcqs.q: The most common oral complaint in a depressed patient is:
mcqs.explain: Xerostomia is the most common oral complaint, leading to candidiasis, accelerated caries and impaired taste.

mcqs.q: Elective dental treatment in a depressed patient should be:
opts: Deferred until the depression is controlled (but start prevention early)
mcqs.explain: Defer elective treatment until depression is under control, but institute preventive programmes early.

mcqs.q: After a patient with an eating disorder/depression vomits, the recommended mouth care is:
opts: Rinse with an alkaline (sodium bicarbonate) solution; avoid brushing immediately
mcqs.explain: Rinse with an alkaline (NaHCO₃) mouthwash after vomiting and avoid brushing immediately (enamel is softened by acid); stimulate saliva with sugar-free products.

mcqs.q: Conscious sedation in a schizophrenic dental patient is:
mcqs.explain: Conscious sedation is safe in schizophrenia; GA is best avoided (severe hypotension risk).

saqs.q: Define mental disorder and explain why oral health suffers.
saqs.a: A clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion, mood or behaviour with distress/impaired function. Oral health suffers from poor self-perception, neglected hygiene, drug side effects, poor diet and substance abuse.

≥2 persistent symptoms for 6 months: delusions (false beliefs), hallucinations (visual/auditory), disorganized speech (loose associations/perseveration) or catatonic behaviour. Intelligence is unimpaired.

saqs.q: List the dental aspects of schizophrenia.
saqs.a: Higher risk of caries/periodontal disease/tooth loss; conscious sedation safe, avoid GA (hypotension); haloperidol blocks adrenaline; raise chair slowly (orthostatic hypotension); neuroleptics → xerostomia, dyskinesia.

saqs.q: Describe tardive dyskinesia and its dental complications.
saqs.a: Involuntary, purposeless movements of the mouth/tongue/lips/jaws in 15–20% on phenothiazines. Complications: tooth wear, TMJ degeneration, impaired speech/chewing, weight loss. Does NOT respond to drug withdrawal — reduce dose/switch to clozapine.

saqs.q: List the risk factors and criteria of major depression.
saqs.a: Risk: female (hormonal), genetics, chronic illness, stress. Criteria: persistent sadness + loss of interest ≥2 weeks + ≥4 of appetite/weight change, fatigue, guilt, poor concentration, disturbed sleep, suicidal thoughts.

saqs.q: Summarise the oral effects of antidepressants/mood stabilisers.
saqs.a: TCAs: xerostomia, potentiate epinephrine (cardiac CI). SSRIs: xerostomia, stomatitis, bruxism. MAOIs: dry mouth (epinephrine safe). Lithium: xerostomia, lichenoid stomatitis, metallic taste.

saqs.q: Outline the dental management of depression-related xerostomia.
saqs.a: Defer care until controlled (prevention early). For xerostomia (candidiasis, caries): stimulate saliva (sugar-free mints, water), soft brush, alkaline (NaHCO₃) rinse after vomiting, raise chair slowly (postural hypotension).
